title: Two-Line Caller ID
summary: A Windows/Python application that monitors two telephone lines, identifies incoming callers and brings their saved customer information into view.
problem: Help an operator connect an incoming call with a customer record without manually searching a separate contact list.
approach: Read caller numbers from a serial caller-ID device.
Stored a customer contact list with address, identifier and optional secondary number.
Displayed matching information on subsequent calls and saved incoming-call records to spreadsheets.
outcome: A two-line caller-ID workflow combining serial hardware, a Tkinter desktop interface and call logging in spreadsheet files.

sections.title: Two telephone lines, one interface
body: The desktop application listens to a serial caller-ID device connected to two business telephone lines. When a number arrives, the application links it to the stored customer information.

sections.title: Turning a first call into a useful record
body: The operator can save a new caller with an address, customer identifier and optional additional number. On a later call, the matching record is displayed so the operator has context at the start of the conversation.

sections.title: A call history outside the application
body: Incoming calls are saved to spreadsheet files for later reference. Python, Tkinter, Pyserial and openpyxl provide the main desktop and data-handling workflow.

sections.title: The hardware boundary
body: A Windows PC runs the application while a dedicated serial device receives caller-ID information from the telephone lines. The project media shows the adapter and a short application test.

decisionNotes: A dedicated serial adapter receives caller-ID information from two telephone lines, while the Windows/Python application matches incoming numbers to saved customer records. The Tkinter interface presents caller details, and spreadsheet files retain incoming-call history.
validationNotes: A photograph identifies the serial caller-ID adapter, and a short application-test recording documents the desktop workflow. These show the hardware/software interaction; no line-compatibility, call-volume or reliability measurement is supplied.
